newsitem.title: USA: U.S. ready for fall-out from any stock drop - Rubin.
newsitem.headline: U.S. ready for fall-out from any stock drop - Rubin.

text.p: The federal government is ready to handle the economic and financial fall-out if the high-flying stock market collapses, Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said Sunday.
"I'm comfortable that we're well prepared should anything happen," he told NBC television's Meet the Press programme.
Stock prices tumbled on Friday, just two days after the Dow Jones industrial average eclipsed the 8,000 level for the first time.
The stock market's relentless rise in recent months has some investors worried that it may have climbed too far and is primed for a fall.
Rubin said that the government had protective safeguards in place to make sure that any stock market dive did not threaten the financial system.

However, he hastened to say that he was not commenting on whether or not a stock market drop would occur. "As Secretary of the Treasury, it is not constructive for me to express views on markets," he said.
The Treasury chief described the outlook for the economy as "quite favourable."
"We're likely to stay on a very good path," he added.
But he said that investors who put their money in stocks not only had to take account of the economic outlook, but also had to decide whether the market was fairly valued given their expectations.
Rubin reiterated his view that a capital gains tax cut probably would have little effect on the overall economy.
"A capital gains tax cut is unlikely to contribute very much to economic growth," the former Wall Street executive said.
Republican lawmakers are pressing for wide-ranging cuts in capital gains taxes, arguing that would boost savings, investment and growth.
In his interview on NBC, Rubin also denied rumours that he planned to step down soon as Treasury chief.
"I will be here for a good long time to come," he said, adding, "I have no reason to think I won't be here until the year 2000."
The 30-share Dow industrial average fell 130.31 points, or 1.6 percent, to 7,890.46 on Friday. The world's most widely watched stock index lost 31.36 points for the week.
